intro.text: You are a hedge-witch from the border village. You read the green lines in the hedgerows and know when the old world shifts beneath them. You learned your craft at the village edge, where the hedges mark the limit of what is safe. When the northern mountains began to smoke, the old road called to you before anyone else did.

description.text: {C02}'s sword is clean, and his shoulder sits easier beside yours. You carry his silence like a second pack, your hands ready as if you are answering for him.
{C02}'s word has gone quiet. The space where his oath used to be is a gap you keep walking into. Your own steps feel borrowed, as if you are paying for a promise you did not make.
{C03} leaves the short cuts open for you. Her trust sits in your pack like a warm stone. You keep checking your hands for the proof that you have not spent it.
{C03} has stopped telling you where the road bends. The silence under her eyes makes your own hands feel borrowed. You are walking a road that has gone narrower without your seeing it close.
{C04}'s claim has passed into your mouth. The capital's name feels heavy and official in your teeth. Your tongue keeps finding the edges of it.
{C04}'s claim has gone back to her. You can feel the page of it missing from your chest. Your voice sounds too large in the space where it should be.
{C05}'s debt is paid in water and names. His road-mark sits in your mind like a clear river. Your feet know the crossing before your fear does.
{C05}'s debt is unpaid. His silence has the weight of a toll you did not expect to carry. Every old road he points out feels like a promise you may not be able to meet.
After the road opens, your hands smell of rope and cold water. The old road has started to answer your steps. The pack sits differently, as if it has learned the weight of the north.
The northern smoke has a smell you keep under your breath. Your boots are split at the toes. The hedge-line behind you has become a wound you can feel in your shoulders.
A hedge-witch's face, still young enough to be mistaken for a child of the village. A pack, a knife, and the northern smoke in your hair.

says.text: You have seen the dragon's wake. The hedge-line no longer feels like a line but a question: what is the safe side when the whole north is moving?

The hedge-line taught you what is safe by telling you what is not. Now the northern road is asking you to walk past the last safe mark. You keep wondering whether that is courage or a slow forgetting.
{C02}'s code has come back into his shoulders. You can almost believe he is allowed to use his sword again. That belief is starting to feel like a place you are living in, not just standing next to.
{C02}'s word has gone quiet. Every step he takes beside you sounds like a debt he is trying not to pay. You want to ask what he is saving it for, but the asking might break the walking.
He follows his word farther than his comfort. You are learning the shape of that: a man who can stand beside you through anything, except the moment he has to say what he is no longer allowed to do.

{C03} has started leaving the short cuts open for you. It is a small, dangerous gift. You do not know what she has already decided to leave behind, and you are afraid of being the reason she leaves less.
{C03} sees the shortcut before you do, and now she keeps it to herself. The road feels wider because of the missing information. You cannot tell if that is safety or distance.
She knows the old roads the way you know hedges, by touch and consequence. You trust the knowing, but you are not sure you trust the choosing in it.
{C04}'s claim has moved into your mouth. The capital's name sits there like a stone with edges. You can feel what it would mean to say it, and what it would mean to let her say it first.
{C04} has taken her claim back. The absence of it makes your own voice feel too large. You keep reaching for the weight she used to carry, as if you might still be owed it.
She carries dangerous knowledge like a weight she will not set down. You keep measuring how much of that weight is hers and how much she is asking you to hold.
{C05}'s debt is paid in water and names. His road-mark sits in your mind like a clear river. You do not fully understand the currency, but you feel the moment you have become solvent in it.
{C05}'s debt is unpaid. His silence has the weight of a toll you did not expect to carry. Every old road he points out feels like a promise you may not be able to meet.
He knows the old roads better than {C03}, and he asks for them in a currency you did not expect. You are trying to learn the exchange rate before it spends you.
After the road opens, the fellowship has a price on it. You can feel the price moving around in your pack. You are not sure which hand you will pay with.

The dragon is not a thing to stop so much as a fact the northern mountains are making. You keep two answers ready: one that holds the fellowship together, and one that lets the road choose who is left.

You want to reach the dragon with the people who came to you. The road keeps asking whether you are the one who keeps them together or the one who learns which loyalties are worth breaking. Both answers feel like a door, and both doors are not the same door.

dragon_recognition.meaning: The degree to which the dragon acknowledges the hedge-witch's lineage as a valid counter-weight to its own waking, rather than a wound to be healed.

eamon_code.meaning: The degree to which Eamon trusts that his word can hold the fellowship together without the sword breaking it.

ellis_trust.meaning: How far Ellis believes you will let her be the one who knows the way, rather than the one who has to be saved.

morrow_claim.meaning: The extent to which Morrow believes the dragon's answer belongs to her, and whether she will let the fellowship share in the discovery.

tristram_debt.meaning: The weight of the promise you owe him, and whether he sees you as a debtor or a fellow traveler.

description.text: A low stone-and-timber house at the village's inner edge, its one room built around a broad stone hearth and a smoke hole cut too low by a generation of mending. A bench runs along the wall, a shelf holds jars of yarrow and iron filings, and the door stands with its iron latch ready for the lane. The air smells of woodsmoke, wet wool, and the green bite of cut herbs. Grey dawn light comes through a small window, laying the room in ash and umber.

description.text: A low gate of oak posts and woven rods where the village path meets the hedge-line, its crossbar notched with a tally of departures. A flat stone set into the gate path carries a carved road-name, and a slate board nailed to the post holds chalk marks rubbed by thumbs. The northern road runs north from the gate, its ruts filled with rain and old cart mud. The air here smells of cut grass, wet iron, and the green pressure of the hedge beyond.

A board of oiled planks above one stall is nailed for road names and traveler's claims, and a rough-hewn bench sits where guides and thieves have waited. The lane smells of bread, iron, and cold water from the well. Its light is flat and grey, with the northern road pressing at the far end like a held breath.

description.text: A broad stone hearth with a blackened rim and a flat iron plate, its smoke hole cut too low by a generation of mending. The stone is pitted where coals have been laid for as long as the village has had a name.
A short cord of pale yarrow fiber, worn smooth by thumb and rain, with a knot pattern that stops one turn short. The last knot is loose enough to be finished or broken.
A low stool with a capital-cut initial on its side and a seat worn to a pale crescent. It has been pulled close to the hearth more than once, leaving a scorch mark shaped like a page.
A pale-bladed sword in a plain leather sheath, the edge notched where it has been drawn against a hedge-line's burn. The pommel is worn to a dull round, as if counted many times in the dark.
A round hole in the roof beam, ringed with soot and patched with clay. The clay is cracked in a star where the wind has tried to pull the smoke down.
An iron latch on the house door, its handle worn to a smooth bar. The catch is set deep in the oak, so it will not open without a deliberate pull.
A low gate of oak posts and woven rods, its crossbar notched with a tally of departures. The rods are damp and green where the hedge's payment has been pressed against them.
A flat stone set into the gate path, its carved road-name worn shallow. A capital's mark has been cut beside it, and an older village debt is scratched beneath in a hand that does not match.
A slate board nailed to the gate post, its chalk marks rubbed by thumbs. The oldest line is a village debt, the newest a capital claim, and the space between them is bare.
An iron latch on the home gate, its handle worn to a smooth bar. The catch is set deep in the oak, so it will not open without a deliberate pull.
A hard-packed road that runs north from the gate, its ruts filled with rain and the old mud of carts. The stones by the edge are worn into a shallow cup where travelers have waited.
A chalk mark on the gate post, a river-city symbol crossed with a mountain. It has been refreshed so often the wood is bare.
A ring of flat stones in the lane, black with old ash and a cold space where a watch should have been. The iron ring is notched where a blade has been rested against it.
A board of oiled planks above a shuttered stall, its nails driven for road names and traveler's claims. One nail is bent back, leaving a blank where a page should have hung.
A thin ledger bound in capital grey, its road-name entries in a clerk's hand and one page torn out. The last open page is marked with a north-pointing notch.
A stone well with a rope and a bucket that has been mended with iron bands. The water is cold and clear, and the wall is marked with names of people who left for the northern road.
A bench of rough-hewn timber, one end split where a traveler's pack has been leaned against it. The grain is worn smooth in a place where a guide has sat for many days.
A standing stone at the lane's bend, its face crowded with old road names and a newer capital's mark. The green moss under it is worn away in a line where the old road still walks.
A shallow ring of cold ash in the grass, worn smooth where a fire was kept. One side is darker, as if someone stood there a long time and then stopped.
A blunt wooden stake driven into the ditch bank, notched with old cord marks. The newest notch is shallow, cut in a hurry.
A thin mark on the stake where a payment was begun but not finished. It looks like a question the wood has been holding.
A low tangle of green beneath the hedge, moving in a slow rhythm that does not match the wind. It feels like something waiting to be named.
The northern road presses against the hedge with a coldness that has no source. The grass nearest it is bent, as if the road itself is leaning north.
A long pale scar where the hedge-line failed, the burn white along the roots. The green under-hedge pulses once beneath it, testing the wound.
A knot in the under-hedge, half loose and half holding. It is the kind of knot that means a debt has not been settled.
The road on the far side of the hedge feels heavier here, its weight pressing through the line. The grass is flattened, suggesting many northern journeys.
A shadow moves along the far side of the hedge, not quite touching the line. It has the patience of something old.
The hedge breaks here into a narrow opening, too deliberate to be weather. It is the kind of place a thief would count before sitting.
Beyond the gap, a hidden track opens under the roots. It is not marked on any village map, but the earth remembers it.
A pale knotted root crosses the hidden track, old enough to be mistaken for stone. A chalk mark is scored into its bark.
A thin chalk mark on the root, faintly glowing where the shadow passes. It is the mark of someone who knows the old roads.
A page held against a chest, its ink wet and refusing to dry. The letters blur where the dragon's pressure has touched them.
A place where an exit should have been counted, but the count stopped. The gap holds the absence like a held name.
A small fire burns at the forest mouth, its light only reaching so far before the dark answers. The flames lean north, as if listening.
The shadows outside move in a rhythm that is not wind. It is the rhythm of something waking, and it presses against the firelight.
A cold breath moves along the forest edge, carrying the memory of a mountain pass. It is the pass itself, held in the air.
The first gray of dawn touches the wet page and the chalk mark, as if the forest is allowing the night to end. It is not quite light yet, only permission.
A page that has been changed by what it recorded, its ink no longer wet but no longer dry either. The name on it will not stay still.
The road has reopened, but only as a lane too narrow for the fellowship's pace. It runs under a name that will not dry.
A single loose knot in the yarrow cord, left unfinished at the village's edge. It sits like a cold promise, waiting to be tied or not tied.

old_road_under_the_hedge.name: the old road under the hedge

description.text: A narrow track sunk beneath the boughs. The stones are packed smooth; boots slide on the wet. The path disappears into the root tangle, swallowed twice over.
A stub of white chalk in oiled cloth, worn to a pale point. A thumb-smudge of blue ink stains the wrapper. She marked things she meant not to.
A shallow furrow in the root-soil. The edges are dark, scorched by bark that turned to ash long ago. The groove runs straight for three paces, then stops. The thing that made it turned away.
A waxed leather satchel. The capital’s seal is stamped too hard into the flap. The strap is worn bright over the shoulder, and the corners hold the damp smell of paper.
A battered kite shield. The village’s old knot is carved into the boss, paint flaking in long curls. A deep nick in the rim shows where a sword, not a dragon, found the gap.
A dead blackthorn with a loop of horsehair tied in the crotch. The knot is older than the moss. One branch has been sawn through, cleanly, by someone who knew trees.
A seam of pale stones set into both walls, older than the mortar. Where the river mist touches them, they feel colder than the wet stone, as if something far to the north is breathing.
A heavy oak door banded with river iron, set into a stone arch. The hinges are thick with rust. The lock is a simple iron staple, forced and re-shod more than once.

A flat river stone no bigger than a palm, smooth on one face and marked with a worn channel where water has cut it. It is the kind of stone the old road families used to count crossings. It fits exactly into the hollow of a closed hand.

A blackened board hung under a warped awning, scored with notches for eels, pike, and salted cod. The lowest row is scraped away so often the wood is bare, as if someone has been denying a debt that keeps returning.
A wooden bucket with a bent iron handle, rimmed with dried salt and a ring of fish scale. It smells of brine and the river bottom. The bottom is patched with a strip of sailcloth.

A hanging sign of a fish and a key, its paint flaked to the shape of a mouth. The key is carved with a road-name that no longer matches any street in the city. The fish's eye is a chip of pale ward stone.

An iron grate set into the cobbles, black with silt and small bones. Water from the alley runs over it with a low, patient sound. One bar has been bent deliberately outward, as if someone has been pushing things through from below.
The flagstone is worn to a shallow groove. A hairline crack runs beneath the arch, as if the road has been pressing against the gate for centuries.
A heavy iron chain hangs from two hooks in the arch. The links are green with river rust. The middle link is filed thin, where someone once tried to cut it without a lock.
A slate board set into the wall lists tolls in a clerk’s hand. The last three entries are scratched out, replaced with a single river-wave mark. A {C05} name is carved small in the lower corner.
An iron lamp hangs by the eave. Its glass is fogged with river salt. The oil inside is low, and the flame leans north when the mountain wind stirs.
A bronze hook is set into the stone beside the arch. Its lip is worn smooth by hands that have held the gate shut in worse weather. A scratch runs across its face like a sword mark.
A carved channel runs along the gatehouse wall. It is filled with black water and the occasional leaf. The water leaves a white salt line where it meets the stone.

A panel of river-oak with a brass ward hook. The lock is cut for two keys: one capital, one village. The hinge plates shine where the door hung in a border house. The grain is scored with a hedge-line mark.
A brass case with a clasp shaped like a river seal. The lid is darkened by thumb-wear. Inside, a rolled chart shows the old road only as a pale scar, hidden under a fold.

A squat inkwell of river stone. The rim is stained blue-black where a damp page has been held against it. The ink holds a cold ring at the surface. The wet letters it has touched glow faintly where the dragon’s chill passes.
A folded warrant in {C04}'s hand, sealed with the capital’s red wax. The seal is cracked. The name inside is worn smooth. It gives her a reason to reach the dragon before the city does.
A bent iron rail across the window. It holds empty page-strings and a blackthorn twig gone stiff with rain. It creaks when the alley wind shifts.
A stone drain at the window’s foot, choked with silt and a green coin. The alley water runs through it with a sound like a counted breath.
A low desk of river-oak. The top is scarred by a pen knife and a circle of cold ash. The drawer is stuck with rain. A capital seal has been burned into the edge.

A narrow window with cracked leaded panes. The sill is worn smooth where {C04} has pressed a page flat against it. Rain from the alley leaves a dark smear on the glass. The crack lets a cold thread of wind in.
A shelf of stone broken short of the wall, its edge split where weight has tested it. The fracture is old, but the split looks ready to take more.
A slab of masonry fallen across the dust, one corner still proud enough to brace a hand against. The stone is cold and faintly slick with condensation.
A long blade in a worn scabbard, the white edge still visible along the throat. The metal drinks the ruin's cold, and the grip is wrapped for a hand that will not close fully.
A threshold stone set into the floor, its surface cut with a name so old the letters are more pressure than ink. The name does not blur in the dust.
The road beyond the arches no longer runs where it should, a cold seam of broken flagstones bending away from the pass. The change is quiet, but it has already happened.
A stone beam broken clean across the passage, its capital carved with a river-city mark no one here has used in years. The break is dry and old.
A dark artifact of stone and older metal, its edge worn bright where fingers have failed to hold it. The surface is warm despite the cold air, as if it remembers being carried.
A page damp with blood and ruin-moisture, its script trembling under a scholar's careful hand. The cold makes the ink bleed, but the page still holds its shape.
A thin green line of letters on the wet page, not ink but something burned into the fibers. It does not blur in the dust.
The narrow edge of the cleft, worn smooth where hands have gripped it. A finger-width of stone separates the lip from the drop below.
A run of ruined steps, each one shorter than the last, leading down into the throat's cold. The stone is dry, but the air above it is not.
A stack of flat grey stones. The largest is cracked down the middle. The top stone has been turned many times, leaving a pale circle on its face.
A thin slab of blue-grey stone. Light enough to carry, but heavy in the hand. One edge is notched with small, careful marks.
A blackened wooden post, split at the top and leaning toward the wind. A rusted nail still holds a strip of faded blue cloth.
Two shallow grooves in the packed road, deep enough to hold a line of meltwater. The stones between them are packed smooth by old carts.
A thin ledge of ice along the rock face. Clear at the edges, blue in the middle. It has formed in the same place every winter.
A low shelf of rough stone where the road bends. Worn smooth where hands have gripped it. A thin seam of black rock runs through its center.
A low arch of weathered stone. Its underside is worn into a smooth channel. The channel is too regular for rain and too long for claws.
A squat block of dark stone set into the ledge. Its top face is flat and faintly warm. A thin line of pale residue runs across it like a dried word.
A shallow depression in the rock, filled with flakes of dull bronze scale. The flakes are old, but they still catch the light like rusted coins.
A length of black iron chain, broken in the middle and coiled in a trench. The links are too large for a horse and too small for a ship.
A narrow shelf of grey ash, packed hard by wind and time. A single dark feather is buried in it, half-burned and still stiff.
A crack in the rock where air moves without wind. Cold enough to fog a held breath. The edges are rimmed with a thin line of frost.
A small folded map, its edges softened by repeated handling. One corner is stained dark. A line of ink runs off the edge like a river.
A shelf of stone no wider than a boot, jutting out from the wall. The edge is worn concave where a foot has rested many times.
A tangle of old roots frozen into the rock. Thick enough to grip, but brittle at the ends. One root has been split clean through, not broken.
A small silver coin half-buried in scree. Its face is worn to a blank. The metal is dark with old sweat and something green.
A short iron rung set into the rock. Snapped at one end and bent at the other. The broken end is bright where it was recently pulled.
A length of hemp rope, rotted in the middle but still knotted at the end. The knot is small, neat, and worn smooth by a thumb.
Two leaning stones set close together. Their inner faces are worn smooth by shoulders and packs. The gap is just wide enough for one person at a time.
A shallow cut in the stone at blade height. Clean and straight. The edges of the cut are pale, as if the stone has been bleached by heat.
A stair of worn stone blocks, each one lower than the last, leading down into the shadow of the far wall. The center of each step is polished by feet.
A flat stone set into the wall. Its face is scored with a line of old letters. The letters are deep enough to hold a bead of water, but the words are gone.
A low arch of chipped stone. Its keystone is missing, the gap filled with packed gravel. The underside is dark with old soot and newer frost.
A line of hardy green shrubs clinging to the outer wall. Their branches are bent by wind but not broken. The leaves are small, thick, and faintly waxy.
The arrow is fresh, cut with a knife. The wood still smells of pine sap.
Its iron rim is bent. The mud around it is full of small claw marks.
A deep fissure runs through the middle stone, wide enough for a dagger blade.
The iron rail is bent flat by weather. The metal is cold enough to sting bare fingers.
A rowan-handled knife with an iron nail in the pommel, for cutting the hedge-line and keeping the safe side safe. The blade is dull from use, not from age.

description.text: Tied with grass string, for smoke, fever, and bad crossings. The smell is faint now, but your hands know the order of it.
A capital letter, folded small, its edge scorched; the seal is broken and the ink has run grey at the corners.
A white-bladed sword lies across the cairn. Frost rims the edge. The burn is sunk into the steel.
The coin is wet and green-edged, stamped with the river city's fish and toll bar.
A length of old rope, frayed at the ends and still damp from the gap.
Cold gray ash, still warm enough to mark the green.
A scholar's page, darkened and blurred where the fire's heat touched it. {C04}'s certainty is spent on the road.
A dry, dense heel of bread, wrapped in a scrap of cloth that smells of the river city.
A small pass fire, banked against the frost shelf. Two empty places by its edge.
The yarrow cord’s empty knot waits where the hedge-line was paid.
A small leather purse with village coin, damp at the edges and smelling of hedge-smoke.
A leather waterskin, half-full, with a knot tied in the neck. It smells of cold river water and old rope.
A length of braided rope, worn smooth by hands that know how to hold on.
A single sheet of capital paper. The ink is dark against the frost, sharp and wet.
A folded page bearing the capital's seal. The answer is written in ink that has not yet dried.

description.text: A short, hard loaf wrapped in cloth. It breaks into four small pieces.

C01.name: the old dragon

description.text: The shadow lies flat along the hedge-line, a long slate-blue bruise under the green. The cold breath that seals the road parts around the loose knot in your sleeve like water around a stone.
The shadow leans over the hedge-line with the weight of a closing gate. The breath at the pass makes the ward stones ring, a dull, iron strike that vibrates up through your boots.
Outside the firelight, the shadow moves in a slow count that is not wind. The roots under your feet hum with a pressure that asks whether you are ready to be named.
The old dragon is not a shape you can hold: a long shadow under the rock, a cold breath in the pass, and a groan that moves the dust in the hedge-line.

here.text: The old dragon breathes cold air over the hedge-line. Its shadow moves along the roots like a hand testing a door.
The old dragon presses its breath against the hedge-line. Its shadow closes over the firelight like a lid settling.
The old dragon breathes cold air over the hedge-line. Its shadow moves along the roots like a hand testing a door.

says.text: The dust in the hedge-line moves as if in answer. 'Your village did not build my prison. It learned my breath, and called the learning a wall.'
The dust in the hedge-line moves as if in answer. 'You carry the same knot as your elders, and you wonder why the mountain refuses to loosen.'
The dust in the hedge-line moves as if in answer. 'The line is not a wall, little witch. It is a scar. And scars ache when the weather changes.'
The groan under the stones settles into a count. 'You counted my breath before you feared it. Good. A name is a payment, not a wound.'
The groan under the stones settles into a count. 'Your capital calls me a fact. Facts do not open roads, little witch.'
The groan under the stones settles into a count. 'I did not wake to be a disaster. I woke because the weather of the world has changed.'
The shadow leans toward the chalk mark. 'Let the path of {C03}, the blade of {C02}, and the page of {C04} stand as witnesses. Then the road will know you are not alone.'
The shadow leans toward the chalk mark. 'You would bind me with the same hedge you call a home. Then the road will close behind you.'
The shadow leans toward the chalk mark. 'The road is older than your village's fear. It asks what you are willing to pay to keep it green.'
The breath over the page slows, as if tasting the ink. 'If the scholar's page is offered as a key, not a chain, I will let it speak.'
The breath over the page slows, as if tasting the ink. 'You have let the capital's ledger stand between you and the mountain. Then the answer will be written, not given.'
The breath over the page slows, as if tasting the ink. 'A capital's name is a cold coin. It buys passage, but it does not know the debt.'
The cold line of breath pauses where the knot hangs in your sleeve. 'Give the knot to the one who can leave. I will accept the absence as payment.'
The cold line of breath pauses where the knot hangs in your sleeve. 'You keep the knot closed, as if the road were yours to own. Then I will open it with my breath, and you will not be invited.'
The cold line of breath pauses where the knot hangs in your sleeve. 'A loose knot is a question. Ask it what it will not say, and I will answer.'
A shadow pools along the wall. 'The knight's rust has become a kind of proof. He carries his debt where the capital can see it, and that earns a place in my breath.'
Stone grinds beneath a slow breath. 'The knight's shame is a loose nail. Strike it again, and it will drive somewhere it was never meant to go.'
A shadow folds along the wall. 'The one in rusted mail carries a debt older than his shame. I do not forgive it; I weigh it.'
The dark under the eaves loosens. 'The hands of {C03} have learned that I do not take what is not offered. That is a rare warmth, and I keep it.'
A shadow slips along the road like a hand testing a knot. 'The hands of {C03} move as if every knot is a wound. Let them learn what a wake knot costs.'
The air tightens at the edges. 'The thief knows the old roads because the old roads know her. That is not loyalty; it is memory.'
A long shadow slides across the stone. 'The scholar's claim is a blade with two edges. If she cuts the capital's name free, I will let her hold the handle.'
The ground gives a low, patient groan. 'The scholar carries a name that has never been paid. Names are coins; I collect the ones that rust.'
A shadow settles over the scholar's shoulder. 'The capital's name is a young thing. It wants to be first. I was first.'
The air smells of river mud and cold iron. 'The river guide's debt is now a rope, not a chain. Pull, and you will feel my hand on the other end.'
A shadow pools in the waterlight. 'The river guide sells what the water keeps. I have drunk his city's patience dry.'
The stone underfoot shifts, just enough. 'The river guide knows where the road is bought. He does not know what the road is for.'
A shadow leans against the memory of the village. 'Your village is a stitch I have been pulling at for a hundred years. It holds because it aches.'
The dark beyond the trees thickens. 'The forest keeps what the hedge forgets. When I breathe, its roots listen.'
A cold pressure gathers at the iron. 'The gatehouse asks a question with iron. I answer with weather.'
Stone settles in the old walls. 'The ruins are my older teeth. Do not polish them for the capital.'

says.text: The pass exhales, slow and heavy. 'The pass is not a door, little witch. It is a mouth that has learned your name. Walk through it as a payment, not a petition.'
The pass seals itself with a breath of cold. 'The pass is a mouth that has forgotten your village. Speak the name I was given, or be swallowed by the one you carry.'
The mountain leans toward the road, its weight settling into the stone. 'The pass is where the old world still has a place in the new. Do not mistake that for kindness.'
A shadow moves where no wind should move it, sliding under the fractured rock. 'The path that hides is the one I am walking. You are not lost; you are being read.'
The air sharpens with the smell of wet stone and cold iron. 'The guide's price is a word, a page, a hand. I take the hand first, because it is warm.'

The ground answers with a long, low crack that runs through the frost. 'The ground did not fail him; it remembered the weight of an oath. Let the thief choose, and I will learn what her hands prefer.'
A shadow rests on the threshold, heavy and patient. 'The home gate is a promise your village made with wood and fear. I have not broken it, only tested it.'

The stone hums under a slow breath, vibrating through the cold. 'A road-name stone is a coin with two faces. Turn it toward the capital and it buys a name; turn it toward the hedge and it buys a road.'
The air turns cold around the thought of the ledger, frost forming on the breath. 'The capital's ledger can hold my name, but it cannot hold my weight. Do not let it forget the difference.'
A shadow slides over the pages of the ledger, dark and quick. 'The capital's ledger is a young hunger. It counts breaths as debts and debts as names.'
The stone beneath the road answers with a low groan. 'The capital's ledger wants to own the ending. I want to own the road.'
The dark presses gently against the green, a cold pulse under the leaves. 'The green under-hedge is the village's oldest answer. It grows where the wall was first bled.'
A shadow passes over the chalk, erasing the mark from sight. 'Chalk is a coward's stone. It washes off, but I remember what it tried to say.'
The pass breathes out, slow and deliberate, steam rising from the snout. 'My breath is not a weapon, little witch. It is the weather of a decision.'
The pass's breath seals the road with cold, a white line across the stone. 'My breath seals what the road cannot carry. If you follow it, follow it as a payment.'
The mountain exhales through the pass, a long, low sound of shifting weight. 'The pass's breath is the oldest part of me that still fits the world. Use it, and it will use you back.'
A shadow falls over the page, darkening the ink. 'The changed page is my name written in someone else's hand. It is not wrong; it is late.'

says.text: The road beneath the hedge stirs, green veins pulsing under the soil. 'The old road under the hedge is not buried; it is waiting to be paid for. Your village tied it shut with green.'
The old road answers with a low, grinding ache in the earth. 'The old road under the hedge is a debt the capital has not yet learned to spend. Spend it, and the road will spend you.'
The road beneath the hedge presses against the earth, heavy and still. 'The old road under the hedge is not a road anymore; it is a memory with a direction.'
The ward stones answer with a dull, deep knock. 'The ward stones are teeth set in the earth. They do not keep me out; they keep me from being forgotten.'
The named stone hums once, low under the road. 'A named stone is a mouth with one word in it. Use it, and the road will know you are not the first to arrive.'
The green name presses against the air like a slow wound. 'The green name is the village's first payment. It is not a word; it is a wound that learned to grow.'
The flat stone answers with a dull, patient weight. 'The flat stone is where the first bargain was laid. I have seen it wear smooth from other hands.'

C01.history: It has lain under the northern mountains since the border villages were raised to hold it in sleep. Its waking cooled the ward stones and turned the hedge-lines into aching scars, and it treats the old roads as a debt that has come due. It is not a destroyer but a restorer of an older, more dangerous order.

C02.name: Eamon Penhallow

description.text: He stands with his sword sheathed, hand resting on the pommel rather than the grip. When he speaks, it is to name the terms, not to demand them.
His hand has moved to the hilt, and his shoulders are squared as if the next word might cost him the group. He gives answers in the short, clipped voice of a man trying not to break.
His armor is still wet where the gatehouse rain took him, and he does not offer to say it was the code. He tests the sword's weight as if checking whether it still belongs to him.
A crack runs through his breastplate, and he has not asked for it fixed. He rests his knuckles on the scabbard throat, not the hilt, as if the sword is a question he is still learning to answer.
He keeps his hand on the sheath, not the hilt, and when the road asks for a word he gives it plainly. The sword is still there, but it is no longer the first thing he reaches for.
A tall knight in dented armor, a heavy sword at his hip, speaking in short formal sentences that crack at the edges.

here.text: {C02} has his sword sheathed and his hand on the pommel, waiting to be told which side of the line to hold.
{C02} has his hand on the sword hilt, his shoulders squared as if the next word might cost him the group.

says.text: 'The code says I yield. The man says I hold. I am learning which one is louder.' He touches the pommel, not the blade.
'I swore a word. A word is not a wound.' His jaw tightens. 'Ask me to hold it, and I will.'
'I broke it. I have not yet decided what I broke it for.' He looks at the sword as if it might answer.
'It stays sheathed while I stand.' He rests his palm flat on the scabbard. 'If it must be drawn, I will name the reason first.'
'You want me to leave it behind?' His hand closes on the hilt. 'Then you want me gone with it.'
'I was not sure I was allowed to use it.' He tests the weight. 'Now I am less sure it is allowed to stay.'
'You want me to pass with an empty hand.' He keeps the hilt closed. 'If the gate takes my word, I will give it. If it takes my blade, I will not.'
'You want the gate and the man.' His hand closes on the hilt. 'I cannot give you both.'
'A sword is not a bag to be left at the door.' He looks at the narrow stone. 'Ask me to choose, and do not look surprised when I choose.'
'The gate opened on a word, not a blow.' He rests his hand on the closed hilt. 'That is the part I am still learning to trust.'
'The door held because I held it.' He does not look at the ward stones. 'I will not ask you to call that a choice.'
'A gate is a question.' He nods at the stone. 'I answer with my body, because my mouth has been wrong before.'
'If my word keeps one of you breathing, then the code is doing its work.' He looks at you first. 'That is enough.'
'You want me to choose between the sword and one of you.' He says it flatly. 'I will choose the sword, and I will hate the choice.'
'I am not a shield for all of you. I am a man with a sword and a debt.' He swallows. 'But I will stand where it is needed.'
'She pulled me out of the stone. I will not call that a favor I have to repay.' He looks away. 'It is a debt I intend to keep.'
'She knows the old roads. I know the code.' His hand checks the sword. 'I will not trade one for the other without a name.'
'{C03} does not lead people. She leads exits.' He says it without warmth, but without insult. 'I have learned to let her choose.'
'The capital may own the name. It does not own the man who bled for it.' He rests the blade against the stone. 'Let the ledger keep what it can.'
'If the page decides the road, then the page decides me too.' His voice is low. 'I will not pretend otherwise.'
'{C04} carries a name that will not dry.' He keeps his eyes on the page. 'I carry a sword that will not stay still. We are both paying for the road.'
He rests a hand on the sword. 'It is not a beast. It is a name the mountain forgot. We go to make it answer, not to butcher it.'
He spits into the dirt. 'If it wakes, it kills. The code does not ask why. I only ask what it costs.'
He does not look at the fire. 'The mountain has already looked back. That means the dragon knows our names.'
He watches the north. 'It does not know us yet. Let it stay that way as long as it will.'
He nods once. '{C03} knows the old roads because the roads have punished him. That is a kind of honor.'
